As wildfires raged in 2018 forcing his friends, family and neighbours to choose to evacuate or remain to protect the land that defines them filmmaker Josias Tschanz knew he wanted to give his remote community in northern B.C. a voice. Tschanz is bringing his feature length award-winning documentary that he hopes will spark discussion, The Fire In Our Hearts, to Williams Lake on Saturday, Nov. 7 and Thursday, Nov. 12. The film follows communities located directly south of Francois Lake and tells the story of ordinary residents, First Nations and firefighters who chose flight over flight.. “At first it was not a film,” Tschanz said noting, he immigrated to Canada when he was 16 years old from Switzerland and his parents live in the area. At the time of the fires that resulted in ferry access being restricted, Tschanz was smuggled through the toxic smoke on a shipping boat with a friend. “It was just to document things and then create a GoFundMe page, and we had a video that would help people that had lost a lot in the community, but then what happened was the beautiful story of the community coming together and forming an organization.” That organization, Tschanz, said is the Chinook Emergency Response Society which is now a national blueprint on how smaller communities can be part of the solution when there is wildfire and they are too remote to access and provide resources and time. This is where the story takes off, according to Tschanz, telling more than just the fires themselves but the aftermath and what happened during that time. article.title: [phys.org] UN warns warming will breach 1.5C as COP31 opens Monday
article.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The United Nations says global warming will exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold as nearly 200 countries prepare to begin the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9. Climate scientists say the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to become the second year to exceed 1.5C, after 2024. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the world must now limit how far temperatures rise beyond that level and blamed political leaders for failing to act. The Nov. 9-20 talks are expected to focus on fulfilling earlier promises to move away from fossil fuels and on funding for poorer countries facing climate impacts. Turkey is promoting a goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Developed countries have resisted further funding commitments, and the Trump administration is not taking part in negotiations.

[ScienceDaily] Scientists confirm global warming is accelerating faster than ever recorded
article.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Earth is warming faster than ever recorded, with scientists detecting a major acceleration in global temperatures since around 2015. A new study reveals that the warming rate has surged to approximately 0.35°C per decade, nearly double the average pace observed from 1970 to 2015. After removing natural climate fluctuations, researchers confirmed the acceleration with more than 98% statistical confidence.

article._excerpt: The Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation in Alberta is suing British Columbia, the federal government, and BC Hydro for what it says are Treaty 8 rights violations related to several dams on the Peace River, including Site C, now known as the John Horgan Dam. “The Province and British Columbia Hydro built these hydroelectric projects without regard for the rights, culture and way of life of ACFN, which includes the exercise of its Treaty Rights,” the lawsuit, filed on Nov. 5 in B.C. Supreme Court, argues. B.C.’s Ministry of Attorney General declined to comment on the case because the government is in “caretaker mode” following the Oct. 24 election. The incoming government is not due to be sworn in until Nov. 20. The First Nation signed Treaty 8 in 1899, guaranteeing protection for the Chipewyan way of life in exchange for allowing settlement and development in the nation’s territories. When B.C. began building dams along the Peace River, including the W.A.C. Bennnet Dam (completed in 1967), the Peace Canyon Dam (completed in 1980), and finally the Site C Dam (finished in 2024), the nation says the province failed to consult on the impacts on the Peace River Delta. And B.C. is now in the early stages of “information-gathering” on another potential dam on the river at a place known as Site E near the Alberta border. The nation says that BC Hydro did not even speak of the downstream impacts during hearings related to the earlier dams, and did not include the delta area in the environmental assessment area for Site C, claiming there would be “no detectable effects” from Site C. But the Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation says it is experiencing lasting impacts from the dams. The nation blames the dams for altering the river’s natural flow and seasonal timing, impacting water quality and interfering with the area’s natural ecology, which affects fish, wildlife and vegetation. A fresh new look at the Cariboo Regional District Library in Williams Lake was recently celebrated following two months of renovations. The branch was temporarily closed in September and October with limited services available through outdoor pop-up libraries to allow for repainting in addition to new carpeting, furnishings and circulation desk. It reopened on Tuesday, Nov. 3 with a grand reopening a week later that included Virginia Gilbert and Frances Supernault of the Williams Lake First Nation providing a prayer, drumming and singing. Speeches were additionally shared by officials including Cariboo Regional District (CRD) chair and Electoral Area H Director Margo Wagner and Williams Lake Mayor Surinderpal Rathor. Wagner admitted she is not in the library often although she does access electronic materials. “But the difference from when I was here last time is unbelievable,” she said. “It’s so much brighter, there seems to be more room, there’s more additions that make it more like a living room rather than a library.” Funding for the project was provided by the BC Public Library Enhancement Grant that Manager of Library Services Jennifer Coupe said they had received in 2023. “It took three and half years to get this project off the ground and it was well worth it,” she said, thanking staff for their countless
